title: Why God became human
hook: Athanasius: he became human that we might become godlike; Anselm asked why a God-man was needed

segments.voice: Yesterday, prevenient grace: grace that goes before everyone, freeing each person to answer. Your line was grace goes before. Did you take the small step you chose? Day one thousand eighty.

A student sits with his teacher, and the student will not let a question go. Why? If God is all-powerful, why not simply forgive? Why come down at all, be laid in a manger, and die? The teacher is Anselm, an archbishop, and he writes the whole conversation down as a dialogue. He gives it a title that is just the student's question, in Latin: Cur Deus Homo. Why God became human. Long before him, a bishop named Athanasius had given his own answer to the same question, in one sentence people still quote. Two answers. Today: why God became human.

Start with the event itself. John's Gospel says it in the King James: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Not a visit in disguise. Flesh. Hunger, tiredness, tears. Athanasius asked what that was for, and his answer, in an old English translation of his book On the Incarnation, is this: "He was made man that we might be made God." That sounds startling. He didn't mean people stop being creatures. He meant what the second letter of Peter means when it says we might be "partakers of the divine nature": God came all the way into human life so that human life could be drawn all the way into God's. A doctor doesn't heal from across the street; he comes to the bed. Anselm asked the question from another side. Sin, he argued, is a debt of honor owed to God, and it's humanity that owes it. But the debt is too great for any human to pay; only God could pay it. So the one who pays must be both: human, because humans owe it, and God, because only God can. Hence a God-man. Christians have carried both answers. Orthodox teachers dwell on Athanasius: God became human to heal and raise humanity into his life. Anselm's argument shaped later Western thinking about the cross. Other answers sit alongside these, and some of them are coming soon. Earlier still, Irenaeus put it in a line today's carry borrows: he became what we are, so that we might become what he is.
screen: `ATHANASIUS: SO WE MIGHT BE MADE GOD.`
`ANSELM: A DEBT ONLY A GOD-MAN CAN PAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with the question why. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to answer it. Just ask it, slowly, the way Anselm's student did: why would God become human? Then bring it close to your own body. Your hands. Your tired back. The ordinary hunger that will come around lunchtime. In Christian teaching, God took on all of that. Let the question rest there, in your own flesh, without hurrying to an answer. If you pray, you can hold the line from John: the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. If you don't, just keep the question company. The bell holds the time.
Why God became human. Athanasius: so that we might be made God. Anselm: because only a God-man could pay what humanity owed.
Your line: he became what we are. Today, the next time you feel tired or hungry, notice it, and remember the claim that God knew that too. Day one thousand eighty.

howItsDone: Christians celebrate the Word made flesh at Christmas and in the creeds, which say that he came down from heaven for us and for our salvation and was made man; Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant teachers explain the why in different, overlapping ways.

notes: Athanasius quoted from Archibald Robertson's translation in Schaff and Wace, NPNF series 2 vol. 4 ('For He was made man that we might be made God'). Confirm exact wording and volume/date.
Anselm wrote Cur Deus Homo as a dialogue with his student Boso; the hook gives no place. 'An archbishop' (of Canterbury): confirm.
'Long before him, a bishop named Athanasius' (of Alexandria): confirm, or cut 'centuries'.

Anselm's satisfaction argument is summarized as a 'debt of honor'; confirm fairness. 'Anselm's argument became a landmark in Western thinking about the cross' and 'Orthodox teachers dwell on Athanasius' are general claims; confirm.
Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5, preface) paraphrased, not quoted; the carry 'he became what we are' echoes him.
